records.title: Correlates of Subjective Cognitive Impairment Among Community Dwelling Older Non-Hispanic Black and Non-Hispanic White Men
records.abstract: Subjective cognitive impairment (SCI) predicts Alzheimer’s disease and related dementias (ADRD). Identifying SCI correlates may identify cognitive risk earlier in the ADRD continuum. We examined SCI correlates among older non-Hispanic Black (NHB) and non-Hispanic White (NHW) men. Method Cross-sectional data were from 669 men in the 2012 National Health and Aging Trends Study. Logistic regression was used to identify SCI correlates, accounting for complex sampling and attrition. Result Higher education (OR = 0.33, 95% CI: 0.13–0.87) and former smoking (OR = 0.38, 95% CI: 0.16–0.91) were associated with lower SCI odds. Sleep difficulties (OR = 2.81, 95% CI: 1.22–6.47), multimorbidity (OR = 2.16, 95% CI: 1.09–4.29), and ADL disability (OR = 4.19, 95% CI: 2.03–8.61) were associated with higher odds. Discussion Education, smoking status, sleep, multimorbidity, and functional status may be important SCI correlates among older NHB and NHW men. Addressing modifiable correlates may support cognitive health earlier in the ADRD continuum.

records.title: Developing hybrid nudges to promote mental health help-seeking in Chinese older adults: A co-design approach
records.abstract: and  Older adults often face significant barriers to mental health help-seeking. This study integrated participatory co-design with behavioural science principles to develop culturally meaningful hybrid nudges to normalise mental health help-seeking among older adults in Hong Kong. Research Design and  Twelve older adults with mental health volunteering experience participated in eight researcher-facilitated co-design workshops structured by design thinking principles. A graphic designer assisted in visualising the prototypes. Workshop artefacts, design outputs, structured summaries, and focus group recordings were analysed using thematic analysis. The study was primarily an intervention development study; focus group data were used as an embedded process evaluation to understand participants’ experiences of co-design.  Co-designers were 75% female with a mean age of 63.83 years. The co-design process produced a set of hybrid nudge prototypes with two design orientations: (1) reminiscence-oriented using metaphors from childhood games to cue autonomy and peer support, and (2) psychoeducation-oriented using relatable vignettes to model perspective taking. Although the project initially aimed to create social norms and visual nudges, co-designers preferred integrating brief psychoeducational and general well-being content to increase acceptability. The embedded process evaluation highlighted perceived learning, ownership, and collaboration, as well as challenges such as self-doubt.  Participatory co-design can support the development of theory-informed and culturally attuned hybrid nudges to address motivational barriers to mental health help-seeking. Future research should test acceptability and behavioural outcomes through randomized or pragmatic trials, and examine how to balance theoretical fidelity with participant agency in co-designed behavioural interventions.

records.title: Atypical survey response patterns as early indicators of dementia onset: A coordinated analysis across longitudinal aging cohorts
records.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
records.abstract: Atypical survey response patterns, such as inconsistent or implausible responses, have been linked to lower cognitive functioning in later life. This study examined whether these behaviors predict future dementia onset across diverse longitudinal studies of aging.  We conducted a coordinated analysis of data from eight longitudinal studies of aging (total N = 76,350). We derived five common types of atypical response pattern indicators from participants’ questionnaire data. Associations with subsequent dementia risk were examined within each cohort using Cox proportional hazards models adjusted for demographic covariates and accounting for death as a competing risk.  were synthesized using random-effects meta-analysis .  Across cohorts, significant associations with incident dementia were observed for item-nonresponse (overall hazard ratio [HR] per SD increase = 1.06), random response errors (HR = 1.25), multivariate outlier responses (HR = 1.31), and incompatible response patterns indexed by Guttman errors and person-fit statistics (HRs = 1.22–1.25). Extreme responding was not significantly associated with dementia risk. Secondary analyses suggested stronger associations among individuals younger than 75 years and those with higher levels of education. Discussion Routine survey responses contain behavioral signals associated with emerging dementia risk. Because these indicators can be derived from existing survey data without additional testing burden, they may provide a scalable complement to traditional approaches for studying cognitive aging in large population-based cohorts.

records.title: Is there a role for artificial intelligence in end-of-life care for persons with dementia? Perspectives of and recommendations by caregivers and hospice staff
records.abstract: and  Tools powered by artificial intelligence (AI) are reshaping many aspects of dementia care, and end-of-life caregiving for persons with dementia may not be exempt from such paradigm shifts. In this study, we explored families’ and staff’s acceptance of AI in hospice dementia care and generated actionable recommendations for AI designers in supporting end-of-life care for persons with dementia. Design and  In this qualitative descriptive study, we conducted individual and focus group interviews with family caregivers (N = 30) of hospice patients with dementia and hospice staff (N = 9). We utilized the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) as our theoretical framework and conducted directed content analysis.  Participants described AI tools as potentially helpful for obtaining information, monitoring patients, managing medications and appointments, providing companionship, and conducting logistical tasks. Familiarity with technology, along with user-friendly interfaces and guidance, emerged as subcategories of perceived ease of use. The uniqueness of hospice, encompassing its humanistic nature and emphasis on families as part of the care unit, also emerged as a key factor impacting attitudes towards AI use. Although many anticipated that AI would bring inevitable changes in the future, they showed nuanced trust and perspectives on how it would impact the essence of care. Based on our participants’ narratives, recommendations emerged across three domains: population-related, AI feature-related, and deployment-related.  Families and frontline staff should not be considered merely as end users, but as key stakeholders whose needs and expertise should shape the direction of AI applications.

records.title: Performance of Claims-based Alzheimer’s Disease and Related Dementias Algorithms in Medicare Advantage and Fee-for-Service Populations
records.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
records.abstract: Evidence comparing the performance of claims-based dementia algorithms across Medicare Advantage (MA) and fee-for-service (FFS) populations remains limited. We evaluated the validity of two claims-based algorithms across MA and FFS populations.  We used nationally representative, linked National Health and Aging Trends Study (NHATS)-Medicare data to identify community-dwelling participants with continuous enrollment in MA or FFS during Round 7 (2017; n = 5,018), Round 9 (2019; n = 4,018), and Round 11 (2021-2022; n = 3,086). Using NHATS probable dementia as reference standard, we validated the Bynum-Standard and Chronic Condition Warehouse (CCW) dementia algorithms across three time points.  Overall, both algorithms demonstrated comparable performance in MA and FFS populations, with high specificity (>97.9%) and negative predictive value [NPV] (>92.9%). The Bynum algorithm showed similar sensitivity between MA and FFS in Rounds 7 (30.2% vs. 29.1%) and 11 (25.6% vs. 23.9%), but lower sensitivity in MA for Round 9 (25.0% vs. 36.4%). Positive predictive value [PPV] was similar between MA (62.7%-70.6%) and FFS (62.1%-70.4%) across all rounds. The CCW algorithm demonstrated greater MA-FFS differences, with lower sensitivity in MA for Rounds 9 (30.8% vs. 46.9%) and 11 (35.0% vs. 49.3%) and similar sensitivity for Round 7 (40.4% vs. 42.2%). PPV varied across rounds in both MA and FFS [(Round 7: 76.3% vs. 71.2%) to (Round 11: 68.5% vs. 76.4%)]. Both algorithms identified participants with more severe dementia.  Claims-based dementia algorithms demonstrate broadly consistent performance in MA and FFS populations, with high specificity and moderate PPV but comparable or lower sensitivity in MA, informing case ascertainment across Medicare plan type.

records.title: Approach to sarcopenia in older adults: a systematic review of dietary and exercise interventions in the primary care setting
records.abstract: / Population aging presents challenges for society and healthcare, notably in preventing sarcopenia, a condition that impairs older adults’ quality of life and functionality. This article reviews the current literature on dietary and exercise interventions to evaluate their effectiveness in managing sarcopenia and explore their integration in primary care.  A systematic review was conducted under PRISMA guidelines by searching PubMed, ClinicalTrials.gov, Embase, and the Cochrane Library via MeSH terms and the PICOS criteria. The analysis focused on randomized studies involving adults over 65 years of age that assessed nutritional and exercise interventions delivered in primary care settings.  Six studies, encompassing 444 participants in experimental groups and 226 in control groups, met the inclusion criteria. Combined interventions, physical exercise paired with nutritional supplementation, demonstrated notable improvements in muscle strength, physical function, and body composition. However, the  varied depending on the study design and adherence rates.  Multidimensional approaches within primary care show promising potential for slowing sarcopenia progression and enhancing quality of life among older adults. Despite encouraging findings, limited research in this area signals the need for further studies emphasizing personalized, sustainable strategies to optimize clinical implementation.

records.title: A pilot randomized trial of a solution-focused, telehealth-supported transitional care program in older adults with heart failure
records.abstract: Heart failure (HF) is a leading cause of hospitalization among older adults and is associated with poor post-discharge outcomes. Multicomponent transitional care programs incorporating telehealth may improve self-management and care transitions; however, their feasibility and preliminary effects require further evaluation in older adults with HF. This study developed and evaluated a solution-focused, telehealth-supported program (SF-TSTCP) integrating structured transitional care, wearable devices, an online platform, and solution-focused approach during telephone follow-up.  A two-phase design was used. Phase I involved qualitative interviews with older adults with HF to inform intervention development. Phase II was a pilot randomized controlled trial conducted in a tertiary hospital in Southwest China. Fifty-six hospitalized HF patients aged ≥ 60 years were randomized 1:1 to transitional care (TC) or usual care (UC). The SF-TSTCP was delivered from admission through 30 days after discharge. Data were collected at baseline (T0, admission), discharge (T1), 30 days after discharge (T2), and 90 days after discharge (T3). Primary outcomes were feasibility and acceptability (including satisfaction with each program component and willingness to continue); secondary outcomes included discharge preparation, transitional care quality, quality of life, and health service utilization.  Fifty-two participants (92.9%) completed 90-day follow-up. The SF-TSTCP demonstrated high feasibility, with completion rates of 100% for inpatient components, 92.6% for telephone follow-ups, 85.2% for wearable device use, and 70.4% for weekly platform engagement. Participants reported high satisfaction and willingness to continue the program. Compared with UC, the TC group showed improved discharge preparation, transitional care quality, and quality of life at 30 and 90 days after discharge ( p  The multicomponent SF-TSTCP was feasible, acceptable for older adults with HF. Preliminary findings suggest potential benefits in discharge preparation, transitional care quality, and quality of life. These findings require confirmation in adequately powered trials.

records.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
records.abstract: Our study examined how social disconnection, neighborhood contexts, and cognitive function trajectories are jointly and interactively associated among middle-aged and older Black adults.  Data came from non-Hispanic Black participants aged 51 and older (n = 1,791) from the Health and Retirement Study. Cognitive health was measured by a global cognitive function summary score. Social disconnectedness was measured by three types of social isolation (from extended family, adult children, and friends) and loneliness (UCLA 3-item Loneliness Scale). Neighborhood contextual factors included neighborhood social cohesion and physical disadvantage. Covariables included age, sex, education, marital status, and living arrangements. We used group-based trajectory modeling to test the study .  We identified four global cognitive function trajectories: low and declining (14% of sample), moderate and declining (29%), moderate and stable (40%), and high and stable (17%). Multivariable models indicated that neighborhood physical disadvantage (RRR=.61, 95%CI[0.40, 0.92]) and social cohesion (RRR=.42, 95%CI[0.23, .77]) moderated the association between social isolation from extended family and global cognitive function trajectory membership.  Our study is among the first to examine cognitive function trajectories with linkages to social disconnectedness and neighborhood contexts among middle-aged and older Black adults. Overall, the  suggest that neighborhood contexts condition how social isolation relates to cognitive trajectories. These findings underscore the importance of considering both social disconnectedness and neighborhood context in explaining heterogeneity in cognitive aging among middle-aged and older Black adults.

records.title: Adiposity and Cognitive Performance in Older Men and Women from the Study of Muscle, Mobility and Aging (SOMMA)
records.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
records.abstract: Aging is accompanied by changes in body composition and cognition. Although adiposity has been linked to metabolic dysfunction and dementia risk, associations with specific cognitive domains in later life remain unclear.  This cross-sectional study examined associations between adiposity and cognitive performance in 769 community-dwelling, healthy older adults (70–94 years) from the Study of Muscle, Mobility and Aging (SOMMA). Adiposity was assessed using anthropometric measures (body mass index, waist circumference) and MRI-derived regional fat volumes, including visceral and abdominal subcutaneous adipose tissue. Cognitive performance was evaluated using a screening measure (Montreal Cognitive Assessment), processing speed (Digit Symbol Coding Test), executive function (Trail Making Test B), and memory (California Verbal Learning Test–II Short Form). Multivariable linear regression models were sequentially adjusted for demographic, cardiometabolic, psychosocial, and behavioral factors.  Greater age was associated with lower adiposity and poorer cognitive performance (p  In healthy older adults, adiposity is most consistently related to processing speed, whereas associations with memory and executive function are weaker or absent. Processing speed may be especially sensitive to adiposity-related differences. Longitudinal studies are needed to clarify temporal relationships.

records.title: The physical activity paradox in later life: does leisure-time exercise modify the association between agricultural labor and self-rated health?
records.abstract: Healthy ageing requires more than total physical activity volume; the context, voluntariness, recovery opportunity, and social meaning of activity may shape how activity relates to health in later life. Guided by the physical activity paradox, this study examined whether leisure-time exercise moderates the longitudinal association between agricultural labor and self-rated health among older Chinese adults.  Data were drawn from five waves of the China Family Panel Studies (2010, 2012, 2014, 2016, and 2018). The analytical sample included 18,050 person-wave observations from 9,449 adults aged 60 years and older. Self-rated health was modeled as a five-point outcome in individual fixed-effects linear models. Standard errors were clustered at the individual level. Agricultural labor, leisure-time exercise, and their interaction were the principal explanatory variables.  In the fully adjusted interaction model, agricultural labor was associated with lower self-rated health among respondents who did not exercise (β = −0.753, 95% CI − 0.856 to − 0.651, p p = 0.082). The agricultural labor × leisure-time exercise interaction was positive (β = 0.898, 95% CI 0.793 to 1.002, p  Agricultural labor and leisure-time exercise were not interchangeable activity domains in this longitudinal sample. Agricultural labor was related to lower self-rated health, the general main association of exercise was not statistically significant in the fully adjusted interaction model, and the interaction suggested that the exercise-health association was contingent on agricultural labor status. Rural healthy-ageing strategies should distinguish physically demanding work from voluntary, recovery-sensitive exercise while avoiding causal claims from observational associations.

records.title: Developing a hybrid intervention to reduce loneliness among community-dwelling older adults in China: a multi-method study
records.abstract: Loneliness is a prevalent public health and care concern among community-dwelling older adults. While cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and social support theory provide useful frameworks for addressing emotional and social loneliness, there remains a gap in translating these theories into structured, culturally tailored interventions within primary care settings. Guided by the Medical Research Council (MRC) framework, this study describes the development of a theory-driven hybrid intervention to reduce loneliness among community-dwelling older adults in China.  Intervention development was informed by a systematic review and meta-analysis to identify effective loneliness interventions. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with community-dwelling older adults to explore intervention needs, preferred content, and delivery logistics. An initial draft was refined through formative pilot testing, with feedback informing the modification and finalization of the hybrid intervention for delivery in community healthcare settings.  Evidence synthesis identified the most effective interventions in terms of content, delivery modes, and contact approaches. In the qualitative findings, participants expressed interest in psychological support alongside physical activities, health education, smartphone skills, and fraud prevention. Perceived participation barriers included time constraints, perceived lack of need or interest, transportation, health concerns, and mistrust and difficulty understanding program content. Perceived facilitators included perceived usefulness, positive group atmosphere, and supportive facilitation and enabling conditions. Pilot feedback led to cultural tailoring, incorporation of locally relevant examples and traditional exercises, and pacing adjustments. The finalized intervention comprised six group sessions integrating psychosocial and practical components, supplemented by home practice and digital support via WeChat.  This study provides a transparent account of utilizing the MRC framework to develop a culturally tailored, theory-based hybrid intervention for loneliness among older adults. This systematic process integrated evidence synthesis, stakeholder perspectives, and formative pilot feedback to refine the intervention, providing a foundation for subsequent evaluation of its feasibility, acceptability, and effectiveness in community healthcare settings.

records.title: Associations between social network characteristics and daily social experiences in later life: Evidence from ecological momentary assessment
records.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
records.abstract: Sociological theory posits that social networks function as enduring relational structures that constrain and enable everyday social interactions, yet empirical evidence linking network properties to real-time social exposures remains limited. To address this gap, this study examines how older adults' social networks are associated with their daily social experiences.  Using data from the Social Environment and Cognitive Health in Urban and Rural Areas (SECHURA) study, we combine egocentric network data (1,474 alters from 254 respondents) with ecological momentary assessment (EMA) data capturing real-time social interactions over one week (5,342 observations). We evaluate associations between three network properties–structure (quantity, composition, and interconnectedness of network members), heterogeneity (diversity in gender, race/ethnicity, and age), and strength (strong and supportive ties) – and four momentary outcomes (number and type of interaction partners, social activities, and being outside the home).  Random-effects models show that larger and more socially diverse networks are associated with greater momentary social engagement, including more interaction partners, less time alone, and more explicit socializing. Both role diversity and network density are associated with heightened social exposure, through distinct pathways. Sociodemographic heterogeneity also predicts interaction patterns, with age heterogeneity linked to kin-centered interactions and racial heterogeneity to non-kin exposure. Stronger affective ties predicted less engagement in explicit socializing. Discussion Personal social networks operate as critical structures linked to the quantity, composition, and context of older adults' real-time social exposures. Large, densely connected, and role-diverse networks appear to facilitate everyday interactions through different mechanisms.

records.title: The modifying effect of work-care role conflict on the effectiveness of carer support: Results from the Australian Draw Care randomised clinical trial
records.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
records.abstract: People who care for a family member with dementia alongside paid work often experience role conflict. This study explores whether work-care role conflict (WCRC) modifies the effectiveness of Draw Care, an online and culturally-adapted carer support intervention.  Secondary exploratory analysis of a single-blind, parallel-group trial (August 2023–November 2024) that compared Draw Care against waitlist control in adult carers from diverse linguistic backgrounds. To formally test whether WCRC moderated the effect of the Draw-Care intervention, we ran a full-sample linear mixed model that included a three-way interaction between time-point, treatment group and an indicator of WCRC. WCRC was operationalised as self-report of missed work or reduced productivity due to competing care and employment demands. Outcomes included carer burden, mood, quality of life, and productivity/ activity impairment at 6 and 12 weeks.  Forty-two of 93 carers reported WCRC. Reductions in caregiver burden due to treatment at 6 weeks (-10.00; 95% CI -19.70 to -0.31, p = 0.043) and 12 weeks (-9.56; 95% CI -18.83 to -0.29, p = 0.043) were significantly larger in participants with WCRC than without. This moderating effect of WCRC was driven by a robust, absolute reduction in caregiver burden in intervention group participants with WCRC over the initial 6 weeks (-7.19, 95%CI: -12.72 to -1.67, p = 0.011), with much of this improvement preserved at 12 weeks (-6.85, 95%CI: -12.17 to -1.53, p = 0.012).  WCRC appears to modify the effectiveness of Draw Care, suggesting that the intervention may be particularly helpful for carers navigating role conflict.

records.title: Associations of exercise snack–related step metrics with peripheral artery disease in older women: a cross-sectional study
records.abstract: Peripheral artery disease is a common vascular condition associated with impaired physical function and reduced quality of life in older adults. Although step volume and stepping intensity have been linked to cardiovascular health, the associations of intensity-specific step counts, cadence, and short-bout step accumulation with peripheral artery disease remain unclear. The concept of “exercise snacks,” characterized by brief, intermittent bouts of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity, provides a useful framework for examining such activity patterns in free-living settings. This study examined the associations of objectively measured step counts, cadence, and bout-specific step accumulation with peripheral artery disease among community-dwelling older women.  This cross-sectional study included 1053 community-dwelling women aged 60–70 years from the Physical Activity and Health in Older Women Study. Step-based metrics were assessed using a waist-worn ActiGraph accelerometer over seven consecutive days. Steps were categorized as light-intensity physical activity or moderate-to-vigorous physical activity. Step cadence and bout-specific step accumulation (≥ 3, ≥ 5, and ≥ 10 min) were also derived. Peripheral artery disease was defined as an ankle–brachial index ≤ 0.90. Multivariable logistic regression and restricted cubic spline analyses were performed to evaluate associations between step-based metrics and peripheral artery disease. Sensitivity analyses were conducted using the lower ankle–brachial index value from either leg as a continuous outcome and supplementary parsimonious regression models to reduce the potential influence of model overfitting.  After full adjustment, more steps accumulated during moderate-to-vigorous physical activity (odds ratio = 0.696, 95% confidence interval: 0.531–0.912, P = 0.009) and higher cadence during moderate-to-vigorous physical activity (odds ratio = 0.967, 95% confidence interval: 0.952–0.983, P  Higher moderate-to-vigorous physical activity–related step counts, faster cadence, and greater accumulation of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity in short bouts were associated with lower odds of peripheral artery disease among older women, whereas light-intensity physical activity–related metrics were not. These findings highlight intensity-related and short-bout walking patterns that warrant further investigation but do not support specific behavioral recommendations because of the cross-sectional study design.

records.title: Exploring the future of digital health services for older adults in Iran using the GBN scenario planning method
records.abstract: Population aging is one of the most important demographic transitions of the twenty-first century and is creating new demands for health and social welfare systems. In Iran, rapid population aging, expanding digital transformation, and persistent inequities in access to care have made the future of Digital Health Services (DHS) for older adults increasingly uncertain. This study aimed to explore plausible future pathways for the development of DHS for older adults in Iran using the scenario planning approach by Global Business Network (GBN) method.  This exploratory qualitative futures study was conducted in three phases using the GBN scenario planning method. In the first phase, five Focus Group Discussions (FGDs) were held to identify factors influencing the future of DHS for older adults in Iran. These factors were organized according to the STEEP (Social, Technological, Economic, Environmental, and Political) framework into social, technological, environmental, economic, and political dimensions. In the second phase, an expert panel scored the identified factors according to importance and uncertainty. In the third phase, a scenario-building workshop was conducted to develop future scenarios based on the key scenario-driving axes, where the intersecting axes formed the basis of a two-dimensional scenario framework generating four distinct future scenarios for the 2035 horizon.  A total of 70 variables influencing the future of older adult care were initially identified, of which 20 key variables remained after consolidation and expert evaluation. The findings identified Governance and Political–Economic (G-PE) support, together with the Technological Advancement and Innovations (TAI), as the two principal drivers shaping future scenarios of older adult care in Iran. Based on these drivers, four plausible scenarios were developed.  The future of older adult care in Iran will depend not only on TAI but also on the strength of G-PE integration. The scenarios showed that technology can either improve care quality and accessibility or intensify inequality and system fragmentation, depending on institutional capacity and regulatory effectiveness. The study highlights the need for a national integrated roadmap to align governance, digital platforms, and health and social care policies toward resilient, equitable, and human-centered older adult care systems.

records.title: The role of gender in informant reports of cognitive decline in the United States and Mexico
records.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
records.abstract: This study investigates the influence of respondents’ and informants’ gender on informants’ assessments of cognitive functioning in population studies in the United States and Mexico.  Using data from the Harmonized Cognitive Assessment Protocol (HCAP) of the Health and Retirement Study (HRS-HCAP) (N = 3,025) in the United States and the Mexican Cognitive Aging Study (Mex-Cog) (N = 1071) in Mexico, we examined informant reports of cognitive decline with 17 questions from the Community Screening Instrument for Dementia (CSI-D). Ordinary least squares regression was used to analyze the gender of respondents and informants in each country for the total CSI-D score and logistic regressions for each individual CSI-D question, controlling for correlates of direct and informant measures of cognition.  There was no significant relationship between respondents’ gender and total CSI-D reports in either country. Female informants in the United States reported 0.57 more CSI-D symptoms compared to male informants while in Mexico they reported 1.35 fewer symptoms. Discussion Our  show that informant gender is associated with systematically different reporting patterns depending on the national and cultural context in which the assessment takes place. The  suggest that informant reports of cognitive decline may represent social norms in addition to actual cognitive decline.

records.title: There must be fifty ways to reduce ageism: A theoretical perspective on possible interventions to reduce self- and other-directed ageism among older persons
records.abstract: Ageism is defined as stereotypes, prejudices, and discrimination toward people because of their age. It represents a substantial public health concern given its high prevalence and extensive impact on the health and well-being of older persons. Although interventions to reduce ageism toward older persons among younger persons as agents of ageism exist, much less is known about interventions to reduce self- and other-directed ageism toward older persons among older persons. This theoretical paper addresses the gap by proposing a comprehensive framework for the development of interventions to reduce ageism among older persons in the second half of life. Drawing on established theories, such as contact theory, terror management theory, stereotype embodiment theory, and social identity theory, we propose various mechanisms through which ageism among older persons can be reduced. The paper explores theoretical assumptions about which interventions work for whom and why to guide further empirical research on the reduction of ageism in the second half of life. We argue that although at the present time, effective interventions to reduce ageism among older persons are scarce, there are many theoretical avenues that may prove effective.

records.title: Development and Validation of the Attitudes Toward Healthcare Providers (ATHP) Scale: A Three-Study Investigation of Perceived Interpersonal and Institutional Ageism in Clinical Care
records.abstract: and  Ageism in healthcare contributes to undertreatment, dismissive communication, and age-based exclusions from care, yet no psychometrically validated, patient-reported measure captures older adults’ perceptions of age-based bias during clinical encounters. We developed and validated the Attitudes Toward Healthcare Providers (ATHP) scale. Research Design and  Items adapted from four validated discrimination measures plus two new items were administered to community-dwelling adults aged 65 and older in three independent, predominantly non-Hispanic White samples (Ns = 223, 349, 361) recruited through Prolific within the United States. Study 1 examined latent structure with exploratory factor analysis; Study 2 tested and refined the structure with confirmatory factor analysis; Study 3 confirmed the refined model and evaluated reliability, measurement invariance across gender, and construct validity.  Study 1 identified two correlated factors, Interpersonal and Institutional Ageism, corroborated by parallel analysis and Velicer’s MAP test. Study 2 indicated that a 20-item model fit poorly and that removing three items produced a refined 17-item model. Study 3 confirmed this model (CFI = .926, RMSEA = .058, SRMR = .057), with excellent reliability for Interpersonal Ageism and the total scale, good reliability for Institutional Ageism, full scalar invariance across gender, and coherent discriminant and convergent validity.  The 17-item ATHP is a psychometrically sound, healthcare-specific measure distinguishing interpersonal from institutional ageism, equipping researchers, health systems, and policymakers to monitor age-based bias and evaluate interventions.

records.title: Multidimensional Losses and Mental Health of Older Adults in Puerto Rico in the Aftermath of Hurricane Mária
records.abstract: Natural disasters often deprive older adults of essential resources such as food, housing, and finances. Hurricane María devastated Puerto Rico in 2017. This study examines the types of losses experienced by older adults and the association of these losses with mental health 2 years later. We conducted face-to-face interviews with 154 older adults between 2019 and 2020 and found that two-thirds suffered home damage, and 47% lost food. We used latent class analysis to identify three typologies of loss: home damage, displacement, and multi-loss. Older adults who experienced home damage reported better mental health outcomes compared to those in the multi-loss group. Our findings suggest that the types and configurations of post-disaster loss can have different long-term effects on mental health, emphasizing the importance of addressing both essential basic needs and other forms of loss in disaster recovery efforts.

records.title: Age, Resilience, and Hope Predict Daily Functioning After a Flood
records.abstract: We examined associations among resilience characteristics, risk factors, and self-reported functional impairment using archival data from persons exposed to the 2016 flooding in Baton Rouge, LA. Three flood exposure groups were compared: non-flooded (controls), single disaster (flooded in 2016), and double disaster (flooded in 2005 and again in 2016). The Barkley Functional Impairment Scale (BFIS), a self-report measure of daily functioning, was the primary outcome measure. The single disaster group reported more problems in daily functioning than did the non-flooded controls. Correlations revealed that older age was associated with greater resilience and fewer risk characteristics. Regression analyses confirmed that age, resilience, and hope were associated with greater daily functioning after key sociodemographic factors and risk variables were accounted for. Strategies for managing the long-term impacts of multiple disasters for people who live in geographic areas that are prone to severe weather events are discussed.

records.title: Implementing Dementia-Friendly Videos in Everyday Care: A Qualitative Study of Frontline Staff Experiences
records.abstract: Dementia-friendly videos are adapted audiovisual resources designed to support care for people living with moderate to severe dementia. Although evidence suggests these videos can enhance comfort, engagement, and communication, little is known about how frontline healthcare providers integrate them into everyday practice. This qualitative implementation study examined the barriers and facilitators experienced by frontline healthcare providers when implementing dementia-friendly videos in real-world clinical environments. The videos were introduced over an 18-month period in two contrasting care settings in Vancouver, Canada: an acute hospital geriatric unit and a long-term care dementia unit. Nineteen interdisciplinary healthcare providers, including nurses, care aides, and rehabilitation and recreation staff, participated in semi-structured interviews and focus groups after using the videos in routine care. A reflexive thematic analysis was conducted, followed by a later-stage comparison with relevant constructs from the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR). A participatory research team, including people living with dementia and family caregivers, contributed to study design, interpretation, and theme refinement. Findings showed that time pressures and staffing constraints limited workflow compatibility, particularly because many residents required assistance to operate devices. Limited equipment and unstable internet access further hindered consistent use. Facilitators included motivated staff who acted as catalysts for adoption, the perceived advantages of dementia-friendly videos over general platforms, and staff observations of positive impacts on emotional regulation and participation. Seeing benefits in practice, such as calming distressed patients, reinforced continued use. The study highlights the importance of integrating dementia-friendly videos into existing workflows rather than treating them as additional tasks. Ensuring adequate equipment, supporting motivated staff, and attending to cultural and linguistic relevance are essential for sustainable implementation. These findings offer practical guidance for embedding person-centred digital tools into dementia care.

records.title: Mapping Namaste Care Training for Staff in Long-Term Care Settings: A Scoping Review
records.abstract: Namaste Care is a person-centered intervention for people with dementia in long-term care, particularly those in advanced stages. However, evidence on how staff are trained and supported to deliver Namaste Care remains fragmented. This scoping review aimed to map training content, delivery formats and support, and training-related outcomes. Following Joanna Briggs Institute methodology, eight databases were searched from inception to May 2026, with additional website and citation searches. Data were synthesized descriptively, and training-related outcomes were mapped against the Kirkpatrick Four-Level Training Evaluation Model. Eleven studies were included. Training commonly addressed core Namaste Care principles and activities, and several programs also included knowledge of dementia and palliative care, as well as communication and relational care skills. Face-to-face workshops and in-service sessions were the most common delivery formats, with some programs also incorporating experiential learning. Follow-up support and practical resources were frequently reported, and family involvement was incorporated into several programs. Staff reactions were generally positive. Learning-related outcomes included greater understanding of the purpose and delivery of Namaste Care and reported improvements in knowledge, attitudes, and self-perceived skills. Some studies reported changes in staff practice, although intended program frequency or duration was not always achieved because of staffing and organizational constraints. Resident, staff, and family caregiver outcomes were mixed and could not be attributed to training alone. Namaste Care training is therefore better understood as part of a broader practice-support strategy rather than as a stand-alone educational activity. However, existing evaluations remain incomplete, with limited evidence linking staff learning to subsequent practice change and wider outcomes.

records.title: Compound Disaster Exposure and Preparedness Among Older Adults: The Amplifying Role of Caregiving Responsibility
records.abstract: Older adults are especially vulnerable during disasters, yet the factors influencing their preparedness remain underexamined. This study investigates whether exposure to compound disasters (multiple, overlapping hazard events within a year) is associated with greater preparedness among older adults and whether caregiving responsibilities moderate this relationship. Using data from the 2022 and 2023 FEMA National Household Surveys ( N = 4,075), we employed multivariable logistic regression to assess the impact of compound exposure and its interaction with caregiving status on preparedness.  show that compound exposure increased the likelihood of being well-prepared, and caregiving responsibilities intensified this effect. records.title: Continuing the Role: Lived Experiences of Family Caregivers after Placement of a Relative With Dementia in Residential Care
records.abstract: Placement of a relative with Alzheimer’s disease and related dementias (ADRD) in residential care is often assumed to reduce caregiver burden. However, little is known about how informal caregivers experience their role after placement. This descriptive phenomenological study explored the lived experiences of 9 informal family caregivers whose relatives with ADRD resided in residential care settings. Semi-structured interviews lasting 60 to 120 minutes were conducted and analyzed using Colaizzi’s method to identify the essential structures of post-placement caregiving. Brief quantitative measures, including the CES-D-10 and the Caregiver Self-Assessment Questionnaire, were collected to contextualize participants’ emotional burden. Six themes emerged: emotional dissonance after placement, cognitive load and decision fatigue, persistence of caregiver identity and responsibility, fragmented systems and resource gaps, crisis-driven transitions, and the need for post-placement support. Participants described caregiving after placement not as an endpoint, but as a reconfigured role marked by ongoing emotional labor, vigilance, advocacy, and decision-making. Although physical caregiving tasks had shifted to staff, caregivers remained deeply involved in monitoring care quality, managing communication, responding to crises, and serving as the primary emotional anchor for their relatives. Quantitative findings reinforced these accounts, with all participants scoring above the CES-D-10 clinical threshold and reporting substantial caregiver distress. Taken together, the findings suggest that caregiving continues in sustained and multidimensional ways after residential placement. Residential care settings should recognize family caregivers as ongoing partners and provide structured orientation, clearer communication pathways, and psychosocial support to address the emotional, cognitive, and relational demands of post-placement caregiving.

records.abstract: Prior research often reports geographic cognitive health disparities in later life, including across rural-urban contexts. This study investigates whether social networks moderate or mediate the association between geographic context and cognitive health.  We use data from the Social Environment and Cognitive Health in Urban and Rural Areas study, which is a state representative sample of adults aged 55 and older. A latent measure of social bridging (i.e., connections to weak and diverse ties) was extracted using personal network data. Cognitive health was measured using the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA). Rurality was defined using the Indiana County Classification. Moderation and mediation pathways were tested using linear regression models.  There were no observed rural-urban differences in MoCA scores. Yet the association between social bridging and MoCA was significantly stronger among rural participants compared to urban participants. Rural participants with the lowest levels of social bridging performed significantly worse on the MoCA compared to urban participants with similar bridging levels. These geographic disparities were not present when comparing rural and urban participants with high levels of social bridging. Discussion The ability to personally bridge social ties within a network appears to play a more critical role in the cognitive health of rural residents, who live in communities with fewer structural opportunities for social stimulation, compared to urban residents.

records.title: Bridge jobs and retirement identities: Gendered life course approach to workforce exits among Early Boomers
records.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
records.abstract: The prevalence of bridge jobs, post-career work that bridges between career jobs and workforce exit, has obfuscated the isomorphic link between older adults’ role identities as retirees, named ‘retirement identities’, and their actual labor force status in ways that may well differ by gender. We examine how gender and Social Security eligibility/receipt are associated with retirement identities, and how these identities are associated with the timing of final workforce exit.  We track bridge job take-ups and workforce exits of Early Boomers (ages 51-56 in 2004, N = 910) in the Health and Retirement Study 2004-2020. We use multinomial logistic regression to examine predictors of retirement identities by gender, and event history analysis to examine the timing of workforce exit at the intersection of gender, retirement identity, and timing of bridge job take-up.  Findings reveal that Social Security receipt is associated with men’s retirement identity formation, but not women’s. For both genders, ordered retirement identities, from ‘not retired’ to ‘completely retired,’ predict the timing of workforce exits. Women in bridge jobs do not always exit the workforce earlier than men when retirement identities are taken into account. Discussion This study underscores the changes in retirement as an institutionalized and gendered life course status passage, amplified by the increasing pivoting to bridge jobs, but with considerable variability in self-definitions of retirement status. Our evidence suggests that these identities serve as good signals of older workers’ work attachments and retirement plans, offering helpful insights for policymakers and employers.

records.title: Forecasting Assisted Living Facility Demand in Singapore: AutoRegressive Integrated Moving Average Projections
records.abstract: Singapore’s rapidly aging population presents significant challenges for healthcare planning and long-term care provision. This study applies ARIMA time-series modeling to forecast the number of older adults in assisted living facilities between 2025 and 2035. Using historical population data, nursing home residency figures, and simulated indicators of disability and living arrangements, the model projects assisted living demand rising from 19,741 individuals in 2025 to 29,443 in 2035—a 49.2% increase. While forecasts are conservative due to reliance on informal care from family members and foreign domestic helpers, structural shifts such as smaller family sizes and reduced caregiver availability may drive demand higher. The methodology highlights the importance of accounting for disability prevalence and informal care. Findings underscore the need for strategic planning to expand assisted living infrastructure, workforce capacity, and planning frameworks. Singapore’s case contributes to global literature by illustrating aging trajectories relevant to other developed societies.
